title: Analysis of Pell Grant Recipients Over Time for Selected Liberal Arts Colleges
text:
Pell grants are a form of need-based financial aid provided by the U.S. federal government to undergraduate students, and do not need to be repaid by awarded undergraduates. The Pell Grant dataset–compiled by the U.S. Department of Education–provides data on the total number of Pell Grant recipients at U.S. colleges/universities and amount of total aid awarded at U.S. colleges/universities from 1990 to 2017.
The Pell Grant data used in this vizualization was provided by TidyTuesday as part of the August 30, 2022 TidyTuesday dataset, and can be accessed here. According to TidyTuesday, the Pell Grant data was obtained originally from the U.S. Department of Education.

library(tidyverse)

pell <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2022/2022-08-30/pell.csv')

liberal_arts_pell <- pell |> 
    filter(NAME %in% c("Pomona College", "Williams College", "Amherst College", "Bowdoin College", "Claremont Mckenna College", "Swarthmore College", "Harvey Mudd College", "Wellesley College", "Scripps College", "Pitzer College", "Haverford College", "Middlebury College"))

liberal_arts_pell |> 
    ggplot(aes(x = YEAR, y = RECIPIENT)) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_line() +
    facet_wrap(~NAME) +
    theme_light() +
    labs(
        title = "Number of Pell Grant Recipients Over Time", 
        subtitle = "For Selected Top Liberal Arts Colleges.", 
        x = "Year",
        y = "Pell Grant Recipients") +
    theme(
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16), 
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11), 
        axis.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
        strip.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = "black", linewidth = 1),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", color = "black"), 
        axis.text.x = element_text(face = "bold", angle = 45, hjust = 1),
        axis.text.y = element_text(face = "bold"),
        panel.border = element_rect(color = "black", fill = "", linewidth = 1)
        )

title: Analysis of Astronaut Mission Duration per Decade and for U.S. vs. U.S.S.R./Russia
text:
Data Visualization


Code
library(tidyverse)

astronauts <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2020/2020-07-14/astronauts.csv')

astronaut_tidy <- astronauts |> 
    mutate(year_of_mission = 10 * (year_of_mission %/% 10),
    year_of_mission = factor(year_of_mission))

dec_boxplots <- astronaut_tidy |> 
    ggplot(aes(x = year_of_mission, y = hours_mission, color = year_of_mission, fill = year_of_mission)) +
    geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.5, size = 0.8, outlier.size = 1.1, show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_y_log10() +
    labs(
        x = "Decade of Mission",
        y = "Duration of Mission in Hours",
        title = "Duration of Astronaut Missions over Decades",
        subtitle = "Each observation represents an astronaut."
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16), 
        axis.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13),
        axis.text.x = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11.5),
        axis.text.y = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11.5)
    )

dec_boxplots









Code
country_boxplots <- astronaut_tidy |> 
    filter(nationality %in% c("U.S.", "U.S.S.R/Russia")) |> 
    ggplot(aes(x = year_of_mission, y = hours_mission, color = nationality, fill = nationality)) +
    geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.5, size = 0.75, outlier.size = 1.1) +
    scale_y_log10() +
    labs(
        x = "Decade of Mission",
        y = "Duration of Mission in Hours",
        title = "U.S. vs. U.S.S.R./Russia: Astronaut Mission Duration Over Time",
        subtitle = "Each observation represents an astronaut.",
        color = "Country",
        fill = "Country"
    ) +
    theme_light() +
    theme(
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16), 
        axis.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13),
        axis.text.x = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11.5),
        axis.text.y = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11.5)
    )

country_boxplots









From the visuals above, we observe that the median amount of time spent in space by astronauts during a mission increased overall from the 1960s to the 2010s, with the longest mission being completed in the 1990s by a Russian astronaut. Moreover, based on the boxplots comparing U.S. and U.S.S.R./Russia mission durations, we observe that from the 1980s to the 2000s, U.S.S.R./Russian astronauts had a higher median mission duration than U.S. astronauts.

title: Inside the Language of SMS Spam: Characterizing Spam Messaging Using Regular Expression
text:
Introduction



Figure 1: SMS Message


Now we’ve all been there. After all, who can say no to a FREE $1,000? Just click the link!
In all reality, you probably shouldn’t click that link. This is yet another SMS spam message. SMS (Short Message Service) spam messages are unsolicited texts—messages not prompted by recipients—that are often sent in bulk to a large number of mobile phones. While often persuasive, deceptive, and sometimes indistinguishable from legitimate messages (like “Hi, I wanted to check up on you”), SMS spam messages can be more than an annoyance; they can also pose serious digital security risks.
Thus, it is natural to wonder: What exactly characterizes spam messages? What linguistic patterns might be more prominent in spam messages compared to legitimate ones? And how can we use this knowledge to better distinguish between spam and legitimate messages?
These are some of the questions this project seeks to tackle.


Data & Data Source
The SMS Spam Collection dataset contains 5,572 tagged SMS messages that have been collected for the purpose of SMS Spam research. Each message in the dataset is tagged as either ham—a legitimate message—or spam, to distinguish between the message types. Moreover, as we can observe from the bar chart below, less than 1,000 messages in the dataset are spam while all other messages are ham (legitimate messages).


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(stringi)
library(patchwork)
library(ggmosaic)
library(scales)

# Import dataset

sms <- read_csv("spam.csv")

sms <- sms |> 
    select("v1", "v2") |> 
    rename(Label = v1, Message = v2)

# Original dataset includes characters that R does not recongize, so let's change all such character to '`' which has no instances in the original dataset.

sms <- sms |> 
    mutate(Message = iconv(Message, from = "", to = "UTF-8", sub = "`"), Label = factor(Label, levels = c("spam", "ham")))

# From dataset, how many messages are ham vs spam?

sms_bar <- sms |> 
    ggplot(aes(x = Label)) +
    geom_bar(aes(fill = Label)) +
    labs(title = "Number of Observations By Message Type", x = "Message Type", y = "Count") +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16), axis.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14), axis.text = element_text(size = 13), legend.position = "none")

sms_bar









The dataset used in this project was downloaded from Kaggle; however, the original dataset was obtained from the UC Irvine Machine Learning Repository and can be found at the citation below:
Almeida, Tiago and Jos Hidalgo. “SMS Spam Collection.” UCI Machine Learning Repository, 2011, https://doi.org/10.24432/C5CC84.
The dataset is also available in the GitHub repository for this website.


Analysis: Characterizing SMS Spam Messages


Code
# Let's visualize message length (includes spaces) per message type

sms_box <- sms |> 
    ggplot(aes(x = Label, y = str_length(Message))) +
    geom_boxplot(aes(color = Label), alpha = 0.5) +
    labs(title = "Distribution of Message Length By Message Type", x = "Message Type", y = "Length of Message") +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16), axis.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14), axis.text = element_text(size = 13), legend.position = "none")

sms_box









Code
# Let's find the median message length for each message type

sms |> 
    group_by(Label) |> 
    summarize(Median = median(str_length(Message)))


# A tibble: 2 × 2
  Label Median
  <fct>  <int>
1 spam     149
2 ham       52


Code
# Median Length of Message for ham: 52 Characters
# Median length of Message for spam: 149 Characters


When analyzing the boxplots and table above, we observe that spam messages have a higher median length of 149 characters compared to ham messages, which have a median length of 52 characters. Additionally, we also observe that the distribution of spam message lengths is less variable and more concentrated than that of ham messages.


Code
# Let's visualize the proporation of "spam" words by message types. 

sms_words <- sms |> 
    mutate(Message = str_to_lower(Message)) |> 
    mutate(
        Free = str_detect(Message, "\\bfree\\b"),
        Win = str_detect(Message, "\\bwin\\b|\\bwon\\b"),
        Claim = str_detect(Message, "\\bclaim\\b"),
        Urgent = str_detect(Message, "\\burgent\\b"),
        Prize = str_detect(Message, "\\bprize\\b"),
        Call = str_detect(Message, "\\bcall\\b"),
        Now = str_detect(Message, "\\bnow\\b"),
        Reply = str_detect(Message, "\\breply\\b"),
        Congrats = str_detect(Message, "\\bcongrats\\b | \\bcongratulation(s)?\\b"),
        Activate = str_detect(Message, "\\bactivate\\b"),
        Private = str_detect(Message, "\\bprivate\\b"),
        Cash = str_detect(Message, "\\bcash\\b"),
        XXX = str_detect(Message, "\\bxxx\\b")
    ) 

sms_word <- pivot_longer(sms_words, Free:XXX, names_to = "Word", values_to = "Contains")

sms_word |> 
    filter(Contains) |> 
    count(Label, Word) |> 
    ggplot() +
    geom_mosaic(aes(x = Word, fill = Label, weight = n)) +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0,1, by = 0.10)) +
    labs(title = "Proportion of Spam-Associated Words by Message Type", subtitle = str_wrap("Each side column's widths on the y-axis represents the relative frequency of that word in the dataset, while the colored areas show the proporation of messages containing the word per message type.", width = 100), y = "Proporation of Messages", fill = "Message Type") +
    coord_flip() +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16), plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 14), axis.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14), axis.text = element_text(size = 13))









The mosaic plot above illustrates the proportion of spam and ham messages containing each spam-associated word, while also providing information about the relative frequency of each word in the dataset. As can be observed from the plot, more spam messages than ham messages contain the words: Win, Urgent, Reply, Prize, Private, Free, Claim, Cash, Call, and Activate. Additionally, the words Call, Free, Win, Relpy, and Claim, have higher relative frequencies than other the words, suggesting that these words are not only associated with spam messages but are also more commonly used across spam messages. Interestingly, the words Now, XXX, and Congrats/Congratulations appear more frequently in ham messages than spam messages, suggesting that these words may not be as useful in distinguishing between spam and ham messages.


Code
# Let's visualize repetition of specific symbols and words by message types. 

sms_duplicates <- sms |> 
    mutate(Message = str_to_lower(Message)) |>
    mutate(
        Exclam = str_count(Message, "!"),
        Money = str_count(Message, "\\$"),
        Free = str_count(Message, "\\bfree\\b"),
        Win = str_count(Message, "\\bwin\\b"),
        Cash = str_count(Message, "\\bcash\\b"),
        Call = str_count(Message, "\\bcall\\b"),
        Prize = str_count(Message, "\\bprize\\b")
    )

sms_dups <- sms_duplicates |> 
    pivot_longer(Exclam:Prize, names_to = "Expression", values_to = "Contains")


sms_dup_viz <- sms_dups |> 
    group_by(Label, Expression) |> 
    summarize(Mean_Repeats = mean(Contains)) |> 
    mutate(Expression = fct_relevel(factor(Expression), c("Exclam", "Call", "Free", "Prize", "Cash", "Win", "Money"))) |> 
    ggplot(aes(x = Mean_Repeats, y = Expression)) +
    geom_line() +
    geom_point(aes(color = Label), size = 4) +
    coord_flip() +
    labs(title = str_wrap("Difference in Mean Number of Repeats for Selected Words and Symbols Across Message Types", width = 80), x = "Mean Number of Repeats Per Message", color = "Message Type") +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0,1, by = 0.10)) +
    scale_y_discrete(labels = c("Exclam" = "!", "Money" = "$")) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16), axis.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14), axis.text = element_text(size = 13), legend.title = element_text(size = 13), legened.text = element_text(size = 13))

sms_dup_viz









From the graph above, we can start to understand the relationship between the repetition of specific words/symbol and message type. More specifically, we observe that spam messages have a far higher average number of repetitions for !, Call, Free than ham messages—although this was the general trend across all the selected symbols and words. This suggests that the number of repetitions of !, Call, Free may be particularly useful in determining if a message is spam or ham, as !, Call, Free have the greatest differences in average repetitions between the two message types.


Code
# Let's visualize monetary values used in messages by message type.


sms_moneys <- sms |> 
    mutate(Message = str_to_lower(Message)) |> 
    mutate(
        Pounds = parse_number(str_extract(Message, "\\d{0,3},?\\d{1,3}(?= pounds)")),
        Money = parse_number(str_extract(Message, "(?<=\\$)\\d{0,3},?\\d{1,3}")),
        Prize = parse_number(str_extract(Message, "\\d{0,3},?\\d{1,3}(?= prize)"))
    ) |> 
    pivot_longer(Pounds:Prize, names_to = "Expression", values_to = "Number")
    

sms_money_viz <- sms_moneys |>  
    ggplot(aes(x = Number, fill = Label)) +
    geom_histogram(na.rm = TRUE) +

title: Modeling Car Lifetime Using Monte Carlo Simulation and Survival Analysis: A Competing Risks Approach
text:
Owning a car can come with a great deal of uncertainty—from the random “Check Engine” light that flashes on an ordinary Tuesday morning to the unexpected accident that takes a vehicle off the road entirely. While some cars remain reliable for hundreds of thousands of miles, others experience major failures much earlier due to mechanical deterioration or collisions. Understanding a car’s lifetime and estimating how much longer a vehicle can be used for are important considerations for manufacturers, warranty providers, insurers, and consumers.
By simulating thousands of cars and their failures, this project will utilize Monte Carlo simulations and survival analysis to develop a stochastic model for estimating car lifetimes and expected remaining mileage. The model will treat car failure as the result of two independent, competing risks:

Mechanical retirement, where cumulative wear and deterioration eventually result in a failure that makes a car’s repair economically or practically unreasonable. That said, throughout a car’s lifetime, numerous minor mechanical issues and routine repairs may occur before retirement. Thus, instead of modeling each repair separately, this project groups these smaller repairs into the overall deterioration process and focuses on the point at which the vehicle is ultimately retired due to mechanical trouble.
Total-loss accidents, where a collision renders a car inoperable or uneconomical to repair.

title: Modeling Car Lifetime Using Monte Carlo Simulation and Survival Analysis: A Competing Risks Approach
text:
2.5 Survival Analysis
Survival analysis provides a set of statistical methods for studying the time until an event of interest occurs. Although it is commonly used in medical research, this project applies survival analysis to car lifetimes, using total mileage as a measure of car lifetime. Specifically, survival analysis will help answer questions such as:

What is the probability that a vehicle survives beyond 100,000 miles?
If a vehicle has already accumulated 80,000 miles, how many additional miles can it be expected to travel?

In this context, the event of interest is the end of a vehicle’s use life, and the time variable is measured in total miles driven rather than conventional units of time.
To answer these questions, this project will focus on generating a survival function and survival curve to estimate the probability that a vehicle remains in service beyond a given mileage. Thus, let’s now delve into survival functions and curves.

2.5.1 Survival Functions & Curves
The survival function describes the probability that an individual or system survives beyond a given time \(t\). Mathematically, it is defined as: \(S(t) = P(T > t)\) where \(T\) represents the total time until the event of interest happens.
In this project, the survival function represents the probability that a vehicle remains operational beyond a given mileage. For example, \(S(150,000) = 0.60\), indicates that there is a 60% probability that a car survives beyond 150,000 miles.
While the survival function is the mathematical function, a survival curve is simply the graphical representation of the survival function. These curves are often estimated through a nonparametric method called the Kaplan-Meier estimator, especially if censored observations are present.4 Below is an example of a survival curve created using the Kaplan-Meier method:





Figure 1: Kaplan-Meier Curve for Lung Cancer Survival. Source: Bioconductor Survival Workshop (https://bioconnector.github.io/workshops/r-survival.html).




For this project, the survival curve is expected to decrease as mileage increases because major vehicle components, such as engines, transmissions, and suspension systems, deteriorate with use, increasing the likelihood of vehicle failure.

title: Modeling Car Lifetime Using Monte Carlo Simulation and Survival Analysis: A Competing Risks Approach
text:
2.1 Modeling Mechanical Retirement: Weibull Distribution
Formulated by Swedish engineer and mathematician Waloddi Weibull, the Weibull distribution has become a cornerstone of reliability engineering due to its ability to represent different failure patterns depending on its parameter values. For this reason, this project will apply the Weibull distribution to model mechanical retirement mileages, which we will denote by \(T_m\). In other words, \(T_m \sim Weibull(k, \lambda)\), where \(k\) is the shape parameter and \(\lambda\) is the scale parameter.
To better understand the Weibull distribution and how the mechanical retirement model will be constructed, it will be important for us to understand these two parameters. Therefore, the two parameters are discussed more in detail below.

2.1.1 Shape Parameter (\(k\))
The shape parameter controls how failure risk changes over time in the Weibull distribution.
\(k < 1\): Decreasing Failure Risk

This represents situations where early failures are caused by defects, and surviving components become more reliable over time.

\(k = 1\): Constant Failure Risk

This is equivalent to an exponential distribution, where failure risk is independent of the variable it’s measured against.

\(k > 1\): Increasing Failure Risk

This represents aging and deterioration, where failure risk increases over time.
There are varying levels for \(k\) values over 1, each with their own meaning and use.1

Because cars generally become more likely to experience mechanical issues as mileage increases (as mechanical parts age and wear out with more use), this project will use a Weibull distribution with \(k > 1\).


2.1.2 Scale Parameter (\(\lambda\))
The scale parameter defines the spread of the Weibull distribution and can either stretch or compress the distribution. It also represents the 63.2nd percentile.

text:
2.2 Modeling Total-loss Accidents: Exponential Distribution
Mechanical deterioration is not the only reason vehicles stop operating. A car may also be destroyed through a total-loss accident, defined as an accident that results in irreparable damage or damage to the point where repair costs outweigh the car’s value.
Unlike mechanical retirement, which is expected to become more likely as a car accumulates mileage, this project assumes that the risk of experiencing a total-loss accident per mile remains approximately constant and independent of mechanical retirement. In other words, the model assumes that the rate of total-loss accidents does not change with accumulated mileage and that the occurrence of a total-loss accident is independent of the mechanical retirement process.2
Because of these assumptions, the mileage at which total-loss accidents occur can be appropriately modeled with an exponential distribution, \(T_a \sim Exponential(\lambda)\), where \(T_a\) is the variable representing the mileage at which a total-loss accident occurs and \(\lambda\) is the constant rate of occurrence for total-loss accidents.
In this project, \(\lambda\) will also be estimated using real-world statistics.

text:
2.3 Simulating Car Lifetimes: Monte Carlo Simulations
Named after the famous casino town of Monte Carlo, Monte Carlo simulations have become powerful tools for estimating possible outcomes when dealing with uncertain events. By repeatedly sampling random values from probability distributions, these simulations generate a range of possible outcomes which can help us understand their likelihood.
Because of this capability, this project will use Monte Carlo simulations to randomly generate mechanical retirement and total-loss accident mileages from the Weibull and exponential distributions for each simulated vehicle.3 By simulating thousands of vehicles, this approach will produce a distribution of possible car lifetimes, which can then be used to estimate survival probabilities and expected remaining mileage.

title: Modeling Car Lifetime Using Monte Carlo Simulation and Survival Analysis: A Competing Risks Approach
section: 2.4 Building a Model for Car Lifetimes: Competing Risks
text:
2.4 Building a Model for Car Lifetimes: Competing Risks
Now that random mileages for mechanical retirement and total-loss accidents have been generated, how is the car lifetime model constructed?
Because a car can reach the end of its life through either mechanical retirement or a total-loss accident, these risks are considered competing risks. For this reason, vehicle lifetime will be determined by whichever event occurs first, or \(T = min(T_m, T_a)\).
This competing-risks framework provides a more realistic representation of a vehicle’s lifetime than modeling either risk alone, as it accounts for the probability of either event occurring.

section: 2.6 Calculating Remaining Expected Mileage: A Mean Residual Life Approach
text:
2.6 Calculating Remaining Expected Mileage: A Mean Residual Life Approach
To calculate the expected remaining mileage of a car given that it has already been driven a certain number of miles, this project will utilize a mean residual life approach. Mean residual life provides the expected remaining lifetime of a system given that it has already survived up to a specific point in time.
To calculate mean residual life, this project will follow these steps:

Keep only \(T>t\) simulated lifetimes where \(t\) is the number of miles already driven.
Calculate the remaining lifetime for each car as \(T-t\).
Average all remaining lifetimes.

text:
2.7 Reliability Profiles
As is well known, not all cars are created equal—some vehicles are more reliable than others, meaning they operate for far more miles before reaching the end of their service life. To account for this variation, this project also studies three reliability profiles: unreliable, average, and reliable. Each profile is modeled by adjusting the Weibull parameters used for mechanical retirement mileage, while keeping the total-loss accident model unchanged across all three groups.
The average profile is studied first to establish the general framework of the model before it is further generalized and extended to the unreliable and reliable profiles.

Parameter values for the Weibull distribution were estimated using Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE), as mentioned in Section 2.2, based on two real-world statistics: an average car has a mean lifespan of 156,470 miles4, and an 8.6% probability of lasting beyond 250,000 miles5. ## Finding Weibull Distribution Parameters based on Real-world Statistics

# Mean Lifespan of Vehicle in miles: 156470 miles
# (Source: https://autorecyclingworld.com/what-is-the-lifespan-of-a-vehicle-in-the-usa/)

  target_mean <- 156470

# Average vehicle has an 8.6% chance of lasting 250,000 (S(250000+) = 0.086)
# (Source: https://fox4kc.com/automotive/the-longest-lasting-cars-trucks-and-suvs-to-reach-250000-miles-and-beyond-2/)

  target_mileage_stat <- 250000
  target_survival <- 0.086
  
  
  weibull_loss <- function(params) {
    shape <- params[1]
    scale <- params[2]
    if (shape <= 0 || scale <= 0) return(1e10)
    
# Mean-Matching terms using Weibull Mean Formula

    predicted_mean <- scale * gamma(1 + 1/shape)
    mean_error <- ((predicted_mean - target_mean)/target_mean)^2     # We divide by target_mean to make mean error equal to survival error in terms of size and therefore representation

# Survival-Matching Term using Weibull Survival Function

    predicated_survival <- exp(-(target_mileage_stat/scale)^shape)
    surv_error <- (predicated_survival - target_survival)^2

    mean_error + surv_error # <- this is what we want to minimize

}

# ---- Optimize: search for the shape/scale that minimizes the loss ----

3.4 Survival Analysis

The risk table at the bottom shows the number of cars still at risk of becoming unusable, denoted as “At Risk,” and the number of cars that have already become unusable, denoted as “Events,” at each major mileage. # Create Survival curve

  ggsurvfit(color = "steelblue") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = comma) +

survival_curve





Figure 6: Car Survival Curve by Mileage.




Figure 6 is particularly important because it will serve as the source for tabulating survival probabilities at specific mileages.
To verify that the Monte Carlo simulations used to build the survival model produced appropriate results, we can compare the simulated survival model with the theoretical (mathematical) survival model. In this context, the theoretical survival model describes the theoretical probability (not probabilities based on simulation) that a car survives both mechanical retirement and total-loss accidents. Because the two risks are assumed to be independent in this project, the overall theoretical survival function is the product of the mechanical retirement and total-loss accident survival functions. Figure 7 overlays the simulated and theoretical survival curves to allow for a direct comparison.


Show R Code
# Creating Theoretical Survival Curve

  # We define survival as surviving both mechanical retirement and total-loss accidents. Because both events are independent, we multiply their survival functions to create an overall survival function. 

  theoretical_survival <- function(t, shape, scale, rate) {
    weibull_part <- exp(-(t/scale)^shape)
    exponential_part <- exp(-rate*t)
    survival_prob <- weibull_part * exponential_part
    return(survival_prob)
  }

  milerange <- seq(2, max(RAWvehicle_lifetime), by = 2)
  Survtheoretical_curve <- theoretical_survival(milerange, best_shape, best_scale, accident_rate)

  # Creating a dataframe of survival values and mileage

  Survtheoertical_df <- data.frame(Mileage = milerange, Survival = Survtheoretical_curve)

  # Overlaying Simulated Survival Curve with the Theoretical Survival Curve created above 

  survival_curve +
    geom_line(
      data = Survtheoertical_df,
      aes(x = Mileage, y = Survival),
      color = "yellow",
      inherit.aes = FALSE
    ) +
    labs(

      subtitle = "Simulated (blue) vs. Theoretical (yellow) Survival Curve"

    theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16), plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 14), axis.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14), axis.text = element_text(size = 13))

Using Figure 6, we can now tabulate survival probabilities at specific mileages to create a survival table.





Figure 8: Tabulated Survival Probabilities of Various Car Lifetime Mileages.




Based on the survival table above, we can observe that the survival probability reaches approximately 50% between 125,000 and 150,000 miles. This means that a vehicle with a mileage between 125,000 and 150,000 miles has approximately a 50% probability of surviving beyond its current mileage.

section: 3.5 Analysis of Expected Remaining Mileage Based on Current Mileage of Car
text:
3.5 Analysis of Expected Remaining Mileage Based on Current Mileage of Car
While the survival curve in Figure 6 and survival table in Figure 8 describe the overall probability that a car survives past its current mileage, it does not necessarily answer a question that many owners have: given that my car has already reached a certain mileage, how many additional miles can it be expected to operate for?
This section addresses that question using the concept of mean residual life, as introduced in Section 2.6. Here, mean residual life values are referred to as Expected Remaining Miles.





Figure 9: Expected Remaining Mileage Based on Current Car Mileage.




Figure 9 above shows the relationship between expected remaining mileage and current mileage across the full range of simulated car lifetime mileages, whose distribution is shown in Figure 4. As expected, expected remaining mileage declines as current mileage increases and appears to follow a polynomial or exponential trend. This trend is clearest between 0 and 300,000 miles; however, beyond approximately 400,000 miles, the curve becomes increasingly jagged and more difficult to interpret.
This jaggedness is expected, as relatively few simulated vehicles survive to such high mileages. Recall from Figure 6 that at 400,000 miles, only 15 of the original 100,000 simulated vehicles remain. Because the calculation of mean residual life involves taking a mean, estimates based on a smaller number of observations are inherently more susceptible to random variation. Therefore, estimates of expected remaining mileage above 400,000 miles are inherently less stable than those at lower mileages, where more simulated vehicles remain. This increased variability contributes to the jaggedness observed toward the end of the curve in Figure 9. For these reasons, and because so few car survive beyond 400,000 miles, it would be appropriate to limit the model to 400,000 miles.
The resulting model is shown in Figure 10.





Figure 10: Expected Remaining Mileage Model with Current Mileage Filtered Up to 400,000 Miles.




As mentioned earlier, the relationship between expected remaining mileage and current mileage appears to follow either a polynomial or an exponential trend. Although identifying the underlying trend is not the main focus of this project, it would still be insightful to get a general idea of which model best captures the trend. Therefore, let us fit several models to the expected remaining mileage data and visually compare their fits to the expected remaining mileage curve to determine which model best captures the trend.





Figure 11: Identifying the Best-Fit Model for Expected Remaining Mileage Estimates




As observed in Figure 11, the cubic model appears to provide the best fit to the expected remaining mileage data and curve, out of all the models shown.

title: Modeling Car Lifetime Using Monte Carlo Simulation and Survival Analysis: A Competing Risks Approach
text:
Owning a car can come with a great deal of uncertainty—from the random “Check Engine” light that flashes on an ordinary Tuesday morning to the unexpected accident that takes a vehicle off the road entirely. While some cars remain reliable for hundreds of thousands of miles, others experience major failures much earlier due to mechanical deterioration or collisions. Understanding a car’s lifetime and estimating how much longer a vehicle can be used for are important considerations for manufacturers, warranty providers, insurers, and consumers.
By simulating thousands of cars and their failures, this project will utilize Monte Carlo simulations and survival analysis to develop a stochastic model for estimating car lifetimes and expected remaining mileage. The model will treat car failure as the result of two independent, competing risks:

Mechanical retirement, where cumulative wear and deterioration eventually result in a failure that makes a car’s repair economically or practically unreasonable. That said, throughout a car’s lifetime, numerous minor mechanical issues and routine repairs may occur before retirement. Thus, instead of modeling each repair separately, this project groups these smaller repairs into the overall deterioration process and focuses on the point at which the vehicle is ultimately retired due to mechanical trouble.
Total-loss accidents, where a collision renders a car inoperable or uneconomical to repair.

title: Modeling Car Lifetime Using Monte Carlo Simulation and Survival Analysis: A Competing Risks Approach
text:
2.1 Modeling Mechanical Retirement: Weibull Distribution
Formulated by Swedish engineer and mathematician Waloddi Weibull, the Weibull distribution has become a cornerstone of reliability engineering due to its ability to represent different failure patterns depending on its parameter values. For this reason, this project will apply the Weibull distribution to model mechanical retirement mileages, which we will denote by \(T_m\). In other words, \(T_m \sim Weibull(k, \lambda)\), where \(k\) is the shape parameter and \(\lambda\) is the scale parameter.
To better understand the Weibull distribution and how the mechanical retirement model will be constructed, it will be important for us to understand these two parameters. Therefore, the two parameters are discussed more in detail below.

2.1.1 Shape Parameter (\(k\))
The shape parameter controls how failure risk changes over time in the Weibull distribution.
\(k < 1\): Decreasing Failure Risk

This represents situations where early failures are caused by defects, and surviving components become more reliable over time.

\(k = 1\): Constant Failure Risk

This is equivalent to an exponential distribution, where failure risk is independent of the variable it’s measured against.

\(k > 1\): Increasing Failure Risk

This represents aging and deterioration, where failure risk increases over time.
There are varying levels for \(k\) values over 1, each with their own meaning and use.1

Because cars generally become more likely to experience mechanical issues as mileage increases (as mechanical parts age and wear out with more use), this project will use a Weibull distribution with \(k > 1\).


2.1.2 Scale Parameter (\(\lambda\))
The scale parameter defines the spread of the Weibull distribution and can either stretch or compress the distribution. It also represents the 63.2nd percentile.

title: Modeling Car Lifetime Using Monte Carlo Simulation and Survival Analysis: A Competing Risks Approach
text:
2.2 Modeling Total-loss Accidents: Exponential Distribution
Mechanical deterioration is not the only reason vehicles stop operating. A car may also be destroyed through a total-loss accident, defined as an accident that results in irreparable damage or damage to the point where repair costs outweigh the car’s value.
Unlike mechanical retirement, which is expected to become more likely as a car accumulates mileage, this project assumes that the risk of experiencing a total-loss accident per mile remains approximately constant and independent of mechanical retirement. In other words, the model assumes that the rate of total-loss accidents does not change with accumulated mileage and that the occurrence of a total-loss accident is independent of the mechanical retirement process.2
Because of these assumptions, the mileage at which total-loss accidents occur can be appropriately modeled with an exponential distribution, \(T_a \sim Exponential(\lambda)\), where \(T_a\) is the variable representing the mileage at which a total-loss accident occurs and \(\lambda\) is the constant rate of occurrence for total-loss accidents.
In this project, \(\lambda\) will also be estimated using real-world statistics.

title: Modeling Car Lifetime Using Monte Carlo Simulation and Survival Analysis: A Competing Risks Approach
section: 2.3 Simulating Car Lifetimes: Monte Carlo Simulations
text:
2.3 Simulating Car Lifetimes: Monte Carlo Simulations
Named after the famous casino town of Monte Carlo, Monte Carlo simulations have become powerful tools for estimating possible outcomes when dealing with uncertain events. By repeatedly sampling random values from probability distributions, these simulations generate a range of possible outcomes which can help us understand their likelihood.
Because of this capability, this project will use Monte Carlo simulations to randomly generate mechanical retirement and total-loss accident mileages from the Weibull and exponential distributions for each simulated vehicle.3 By simulating thousands of vehicles, this approach will produce a distribution of possible car lifetimes, which can then be used to estimate survival probabilities and expected remaining mileage.

title: Modeling Car Lifetime Using Monte Carlo Simulation and Survival Analysis: A Competing Risks Approach
section: 2.4 Building a Model for Car Lifetimes: Competing Risks
text:
2.4 Building a Model for Car Lifetimes: Competing Risks
Now that random mileages for mechanical retirement and total-loss accidents have been generated, how is the car lifetime model constructed?
Because a car can reach the end of its life through either mechanical retirement or a total-loss accident, these risks are considered competing risks. For this reason, vehicle lifetime will be determined by whichever event occurs first, or \(T = min(T_m, T_a)\).
This competing-risks framework provides a more realistic representation of a vehicle’s lifetime than modeling either risk alone, as it accounts for the probability of either event occurring.

title: Modeling Car Lifetime Using Monte Carlo Simulation and Survival Analysis: A Competing Risks Approach
text:
2.5 Survival Analysis
Survival analysis provides a set of statistical methods for studying the time until an event of interest occurs. Although it is commonly used in medical research, this project applies survival analysis to car lifetimes, using total mileage as a measure of car lifetime. Specifically, survival analysis will help answer questions such as:

What is the probability that a vehicle survives beyond 100,000 miles?
If a vehicle has already accumulated 80,000 miles, how many additional miles can it be expected to travel?

In this context, the event of interest is the end of a vehicle’s use life, and the time variable is measured in total miles driven rather than conventional units of time.
To answer these questions, this project will focus on generating a survival function and survival curve to estimate the probability that a vehicle remains in service beyond a given mileage. Thus, let’s now delve into survival functions and curves.

2.5.1 Survival Functions & Curves
The survival function describes the probability that an individual or system survives beyond a given time \(t\). Mathematically, it is defined as: \(S(t) = P(T > t)\) where \(T\) represents the total time until the event of interest happens.
In this project, the survival function represents the probability that a vehicle remains operational beyond a given mileage. For example, \(S(150,000) = 0.60\), indicates that there is a 60% probability that a car survives beyond 150,000 miles.
While the survival function is the mathematical function, a survival curve is simply the graphical representation of the survival function. These curves are often estimated through a nonparametric method called the Kaplan-Meier estimator, especially if censored observations are present.4 Below is an example of a survival curve created using the Kaplan-Meier method:





Figure 1: Kaplan-Meier Curve for Lung Cancer Survival. Source: Bioconductor Survival Workshop (https://bioconnector.github.io/workshops/r-survival.html).




For this project, the survival curve is expected to decrease as mileage increases because major vehicle components, such as engines, transmissions, and suspension systems, deteriorate with use, increasing the likelihood of vehicle failure.

title: Modeling Car Lifetime Using Monte Carlo Simulation and Survival Analysis: A Competing Risks Approach
section: 2.6 Calculating Remaining Expected Mileage: A Mean Residual Life Approach
text:
2.6 Calculating Remaining Expected Mileage: A Mean Residual Life Approach
To calculate the expected remaining mileage of a car given that it has already been driven a certain number of miles, this project will utilize a mean residual life approach. Mean residual life provides the expected remaining lifetime of a system given that it has already survived up to a specific point in time.
To calculate mean residual life, this project will follow these steps:

Keep only \(T>t\) simulated lifetimes where \(t\) is the number of miles already driven.
Calculate the remaining lifetime for each car as \(T-t\).
Average all remaining lifetimes.

section: 3.1 Weibull Distribution for Mechanical Retirement Mileage
text:
3.1 Weibull Distribution for Mechanical Retirement Mileage
Parameter values for the Weibull distribution were solved numerically (Nelder-Mead) using two real-world statistics: an average car has a mean lifespan of 156,470 miles5, and an 8.6% probability of lasting beyond 250,000 miles6. These two statistics were used to solve for the shape and scale parameters, yielding:

\(k\) = 2.566597
\(\lambda\) = 176,229.10



Show R Code
## Finding Weibull Distribution Parameters based on Real-world Statistics

# Mean Lifespan of Vehicle in miles: 156470 miles
# (Source: https://autorecyclingworld.com/what-is-the-lifespan-of-a-vehicle-in-the-usa/)

  target_mean <- 156470

# Average vehicle has an 8.6% chance of lasting 250,000 (S(250000+) = 0.086)
# (Source: https://fox4kc.com/automotive/the-longest-lasting-cars-trucks-and-suvs-to-reach-250000-miles-and-beyond-2/)

  target_mileage_stat <- 250000
  target_survival <- 0.086
  
  
  weibull_loss <- function(params) {
    shape <- params[1]
    scale <- params[2]
    if (shape <= 0 || scale <= 0) return(1e10)
    
# Mean-Matching terms using Weibull Mean Formula

    predicted_mean <- scale * gamma(1 + 1/shape)
    mean_error <- ((predicted_mean - target_mean)/target_mean)^2     # We divide by target_mean to make mean error equal to survival error in terms of size and therefore representation

# Survival-Matching Term using Weibull Survival Function

    predicated_survival <- exp(-(target_mileage_stat/scale)^shape)
    surv_error <- (predicated_survival - target_survival)^2

    mean_error + surv_error # <- this is what we want to minimize

}

# ---- Optimize: search for the shape/scale that minimizes the loss ----

  fit <- optim(par = c(3, 180000), fn = weibull_loss, method = "Nelder-Mead",
               control = list(maxit = 30000, reltol = 1e-14))

  best_shape <- fit$par[1]
  best_scale <- fit$par[2]

# Based on this optimization, a scale value of 176229.10 and a shape value of 2.566597 are the best Weibull parameter values when considering the statistics that are known and that we have


# ---- Double Checking ----


  best_scale * gamma(1 + 1/best_shape) # = 156470
  
  exp(-(target_mileage_stat/best_scale)^best_shape) # = 0.086


With these parameter estimates, we can construct the Weibull distribution used to generate simulated mechanical retirement mileages, shown below.

section: 3.2 Exponential Distribution for Total-loss Accident Mileage
text:
3.2 Exponential Distribution for Total-loss Accident Mileage

3.2.1 Parameter (\(\lambda\))
Like the parameter values for the Weibull distribution, the parameter value for the exponential distribution was guided by three real-world statistics:

Among U.S. collision insurance claims, there is a total-loss claim frequency of 27%.7
Average collision claim frequency is once every 17.9 years.8
U.S. drivers drive an average of 13,476 annual miles.9

Using these three real-world statistics, the rate parameter, \(\lambda\), of the exponential distribution was estimated to be 0.000001119308.


Show R Code
## Finding Exponential Distribution Rate Parameter based on Available Statistics

# Total Loss Frequency of Accidents of U.S. collision insurance claims in which Vehicle was Totaled
# (Source:https://www.axios.com/2025/03/03/auto-insurance-vehicles-cars-trucks-suvs)

claims_prop <- 0.27

# Average Number of Years a Car Owner Reports a Collision
# (Source: https://www.ppdlawoffice.com/blog/2020/09/average-number-of-car-accidents-in-a-lifetime-and-avoiding-them/)

avg_years <- 17.9

# Average Annual Miles Driven by Drivers in U.S.
# (Source: https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/ohim/onh00/bar8.htm)

avg_miles <- 13476

# Calculating Rate Needed for Exponential Distribution

avg_miles_between_any_collision <- avg_miles * avg_years

prop_totaled_collisions <- 1/claims_prop      # A totaled collision happens every (prop_totaled_collisions) collision

avg_miles_between_totaled_collision <- avg_miles_between_any_collision * prop_totaled_collisions

accident_rate <- 1/avg_miles_between_totaled_collision

# ---- Findings ----

  # Miles between any claimed accident: 241220.40 
  # Miles between total-loss accidents: 893408.90 
  # Exponential rate parameter: 1.119308e-06
    # Should make sense as most accidents do not lead to the complete demolition of cars

# ---- Findings ----

  # It should be noted that the claims proportion for total-loss has been high the past couple of years due to increases in cost of parts and other post-COVID factors. Thus, although the rate calculated here is small, it is actually larger than in other previous years. 
  # Additionally, we must note that not all crashes/accidents are claimed by drivers, thus it is possible that this total-loss claims rate is inflated.


Interpretation: Because \(\lambda\) has a direct interpretation in this context, a \(\lambda\) of 0.000001119308 implies that approximately 1.12 total-loss accidents are expected to occur per million miles driven, or equivalently, that across a large population of cars, the average number of miles a car drives before experiencing a total-loss accident is approximately 893,408.90 miles.
It is important to notice the particularly high mileage between total-loss accidents, indicating that the rate of occurrence of total-loss accidents is low. This is not entirely incorrect, as total-loss accidents represent relatively uncommon events: while collisions occur frequently, most accidents do not result in a vehicle being declared a total loss.
On the other hand, this result may also seem contradictory, as the real-world statistic used suggests that 27% of insurance claims are total-loss claims (not as uncommon as thought). However, it is important to recognize that this statistic is measured within an insurance claims context rather than in relation to vehicle mileage. Thus, the two statistics describe total-loss accidents within different contexts and should not be directly compared.


3.2.2 Exponential Distribution
With a \(\lambda\) of 0.000001119308, we produce the following exponential distribution.

3.5 Analysis of Expected Remaining Mileage Based on Current Mileage of Car
While the survival curve in Figure 6 and survival table in Figure 8 describe the overall probability that a car survives past its current mileage, it does not necessarily answer a question that many owners have: given that my car has already reached a certain mileage, how many additional miles can it be expected to operate for?
This section addresses that question using the concept of mean residual life, as introduced in Section 2.6. Here, mean residual life values are referred to as Expected Remaining Miles.





Figure 9: Expected Remaining Mileage Based on Current Car Mileage.




Figure 9 above shows the relationship between expected remaining mileage and current mileage across the full range of simulated car lifetime mileages, whose distribution is shown in Figure 4. As expected, expected remaining mileage declines as current mileage increases and appears to follow a polynomial or exponential trend. This trend is clearest between 0 and 300,000 miles; however, beyond approximately 400,000 miles, the curve becomes increasingly jagged and more difficult to interpret.
This jaggedness is expected, as relatively few simulated vehicles survive to such high mileages. Recall from Figure 6 that at 400,000 miles, only 15 of the original 100,000 simulated vehicles remain. Because the calculation of mean residual life involves taking a mean, estimates based on a smaller number of observations are inherently more susceptible to random variation. Therefore, estimates of expected remaining mileage above 400,000 miles are inherently less stable than those at lower mileages, where more simulated vehicles remain. This increased variability contributes to the jaggedness observed toward the end of the curve in Figure 9. For these reasons, and because so few car survive beyond 400,000 miles, it would be appropriate to limit the model to 400,000 miles.
The resulting model is shown in Figure 10.

Although identifying the underlying trend is not the main focus of this project, it would still be insightful to get a general idea of which model best captures the trend. Therefore, let us fit several models to the expected remaining mileage data and visually compare their fits to the expected remaining mileage curve to determine which model best captures the trend.

title: Modeling Car Lifetime Using Monte Carlo Simulation and Survival Analysis: A Competing Risks Approach
text:
Owning a car can come with a great deal of uncertainty—from the random “Check Engine” light that flashes on an ordinary Tuesday morning to the unexpected accident that takes a vehicle off the road entirely. While some cars remain reliable for hundreds of thousands of miles, others experience major failures much earlier due to mechanical deterioration or collisions. Understanding a car’s lifetime and estimating how much longer a vehicle can be used for are important considerations for manufacturers, warranty providers, insurers, and consumers.
By simulating thousands of cars and their failures, this project will utilize Monte Carlo simulations and survival analysis to develop a stochastic model for estimating car lifetimes and expected remaining mileage. The model will treat car failure as the result of two independent, competing risks:

Mechanical retirement, where cumulative wear and deterioration eventually result in a failure that makes a car’s repair economically or practically unreasonable. That said, throughout a car’s lifetime, numerous minor mechanical issues and routine repairs may occur before retirement. Thus, instead of modeling each repair separately, this project groups these smaller repairs into the overall deterioration process and focuses on the point at which the vehicle is ultimately retired due to mechanical trouble.
Total-loss accidents, where a collision renders a car inoperable or uneconomical to repair.

title: Modeling Car Lifetime Using Monte Carlo Simulation and Survival Analysis: A Competing Risks Approach
text:
Modeling Mechanical Retirement: Weibull Distribution
Formulated by Swedish engineer and mathematician Waloddi Weibull, the Weibull distribution has become a cornerstone of reliability engineering due to its ability to represent different failure patterns depending on its parameter values. For this reason, this project will apply the Weibull distribution to model mechanical retirement mileages, which we will denote by \(T_m\). In other words, \(T_m \sim Weibull(k, \lambda)\), where \(k\) is the shape parameter and \(\lambda\) is the scale parameter.
To better understand the Weibull distribution and how the mechanical retirement model will be constructed, it will be important for us to understand these two parameters. Therefore, the two parameters are discussed more in detail below.

Shape Parameter (\(k\))
The shape parameter controls how failure risk changes over time in the Weibull distribution.
\(k < 1\): Decreasing Failure Risk

This represents situations where early failures are caused by defects, and surviving components become more reliable over time.

\(k = 1\): Constant Failure Risk

This is equivalent to an exponential distribution, where failure risk is independent of the variable it’s measured against.

\(k > 1\): Increasing Failure Risk

This represents aging and deterioration, where failure risk increases over time.
There are varying levels for \(k\) values over 1, each with their own meaning and use.1

Because cars generally become more likely to experience mechanical issues as mileage increases (as mechanical parts age and wear out with more use), this project will use a Weibull distribution with \(k > 1\).


Scale Parameter (\(\lambda\))
The scale parameter defines the spread of the Weibull distribution and can either stretch or compress the distribution. It also represents the 63.2nd percentile.

title: Modeling Car Lifetime Using Monte Carlo Simulation and Survival Analysis: A Competing Risks Approach
text:
Modeling Total-loss Accidents: Exponential Distribution
Mechanical deterioration is not the only reason vehicles stop operating. A car may also be destroyed through a total-loss accident, defined as an accident that results in irreparable damage or damage to the point where repair costs outweigh the car’s value.
Unlike mechanical retirement, which is expected to become more likely as a car accumulates mileage, this project assumes that the risk of experiencing a total-loss accident per mile remains approximately constant and independent of mechanical retirement. In other words, the model assumes that the rate of total-loss accidents does not change with accumulated mileage and that the occurrence of a total-loss accident is independent of the mechanical retirement process.2
Because of these assumptions, the mileage at which total-loss accidents occur can be appropriately modeled with an exponential distribution, \(T_a \sim Exponential(\lambda)\), where \(T_a\) is the variable representing the mileage at which a total-loss accident occurs and \(\lambda\) is the constant rate of occurrence for total-loss accidents.
In this project, \(\lambda\) will also be estimated using real-world statistics.

section: Simulating Car Lifetimes: Monte Carlo Simulations
text:
Simulating Car Lifetimes: Monte Carlo Simulations
Named after the famous casino town of Monte Carlo, Monte Carlo simulations have become powerful tools for estimating possible outcomes when dealing with uncertain events. By repeatedly sampling random values from probability distributions, these simulations generate a range of possible outcomes which can help us understand their likelihood.
Because of this capability, this project will use Monte Carlo simulations to randomly generate mechanical retirement and total-loss accident mileages from the Weibull and exponential distributions for each simulated vehicle.3 By simulating thousands of vehicles, this approach will produce a distribution of possible car lifetimes, which can then be used to estimate survival probabilities and expected remaining mileage.

section: Building a Model for Car Lifetimes: Competing Risks
text:
Building a Model for Car Lifetimes: Competing Risks
Now that random mileages for mechanical retirement and total-loss accidents have been generated, how is the car lifetime model constructed?
Because a car can reach the end of its life through either mechanical retirement or a total-loss accident, these risks are considered competing risks. For this reason, vehicle lifetime will be determined by whichever event occurs first, or \(T = min(T_m, T_a)\).
This competing-risks framework provides a more realistic representation of a vehicle’s lifetime than modeling either risk alone, as it accounts for the probability of either event occurring.

title: Modeling Car Lifetime Using Monte Carlo Simulation and Survival Analysis: A Competing Risks Approach
text:
Survival Analysis
Survival analysis provides a set of statistical methods for studying the time until an event of interest occurs. Although it is commonly used in medical research, this project applies survival analysis to car lifetimes, using total mileage as a measure of car lifetime. Specifically, survival analysis will help answer questions such as:

What is the probability that a vehicle survives beyond 100,000 miles?
If a vehicle has already accumulated 80,000 miles, how many additional miles can it be expected to travel?

In this context, the event of interest is the end of a vehicle’s use life, and the time variable is measured in total miles driven rather than conventional units of time.
To answer these questions, this project will focus on generating a survival function and survival curve to estimate the probability that a vehicle remains in service beyond a given mileage. Thus, let’s now delve into survival functions and curves.

Survival Functions & Curves
The survival function describes the probability that an individual or system survives beyond a given time \(t\). Mathematically, it is defined as: \(S(t) = P(T > t)\) where \(T\) represents the total time until the event of interest happens.
In this project, the survival function represents the probability that a vehicle remains operational beyond a given mileage. For example, \(S(150,000) = 0.60\), indicates that there is a 60% probability that a car survives beyond 150,000 miles.
While the survival function is the mathematical function, a survival curve is simply the graphical representation of the survival function. These curves are often estimated through a nonparametric method called the Kaplan-Meier estimator, especially if censored observations are present.4 Below is an example of a survival curve created using the Kaplan-Meier method:





Kaplan-Meier Curve for Lung Cancer Survival. Source: Bioconductor Survival Workshop (https://bioconnector.github.io/workshops/r-survival.html).




For this project, the survival curve is expected to decrease as mileage increases because major vehicle components, such as engines, transmissions, and suspension systems, deteriorate with use, increasing the likelihood of vehicle failure.

section: Calculating Remaining Expected Mileage: A Mean Residual Life Approach
text:
Calculating Remaining Expected Mileage: A Mean Residual Life Approach
To calculate the expected remaining mileage of a car given that it has already been driven a certain number of miles, this project will utilize a mean residual life approach. Mean residual life provides the expected remaining lifetime of a system given that it has already survived up to a specific point in time.
To calculate mean residual life, this project will follow these steps:

Keep only \(T>t\) simulated lifetimes where \(t\) is the number of miles already driven.
Calculate the remaining lifetime for each car as \(T-t\).
Average all remaining lifetimes.

Exponential Distribution for Total-loss Accident Mileage

Parameter (\(\lambda\))
Like the parameter values for the Weibull distribution, the parameter value for the exponential distribution was guided by three real-world statistics:

Among U.S. collision insurance claims, there is a total-loss claim frequency of 27%.7
Average collision claim frequency is once every 17.9 years.8
U.S. drivers drive an average of 13,476 annual miles.9

Using these three real-world statistics, the rate parameter, \(\lambda\), of the exponential distribution was estimated to be 0.000001119308.
Interpretation: Because \(\lambda\) has a direct interpretation in this context, a \(\lambda\) of 0.000001119308 implies that approximately 1.12 total-loss accidents are expected to occur per million miles driven, or equivalently, that across a large population of cars, the average number of miles a car drives before experiencing a total-loss accident is approximately 893,408.90 miles.
It is important to notice the particularly high mileage between total-loss accidents, indicating that the rate of occurrence of total-loss accidents is low. This is not entirely incorrect, as total-loss accidents represent relatively uncommon events: while collisions occur frequently, most accidents do not result in a vehicle being declared a total loss.
On the other hand, this result may also seem contradictory, as the real-world statistic used suggests that 27% of insurance claims are total-loss claims (not as uncommon as thought). However, it is important to recognize that this statistic is measured within an insurance claims context rather than in relation to vehicle mileage. Thus, the two statistics describe total-loss accidents within different contexts and should not be directly compared.

Based on the survival table above, we can observe that the survival probability reaches approximately 50% between 125,000 and 150,000 miles. This means that a vehicle with a mileage between 125,000 and 150,000 miles has approximately a 50% probability of surviving beyond its current mileage.

title: Modeling Car Lifetime Using Monte Carlo Simulation and Survival Analysis: A Competing Risks Approach
section: Analysis of Expected Remaining Mileage Based on Current Mileage of Car
text:
Analysis of Expected Remaining Mileage Based on Current Mileage of Car
While the survival curve in Figure 6 and survival table in Figure 8 describe the overall probability that a car survives past its current mileage, it does not necessarily answer a question that many owners have: given that my car has already reached a certain mileage, how many additional miles can it be expected to operate for?
This section addresses that question using the concept of mean residual life, as introduced in Section 2.6. Here, mean residual life values are referred to as Expected Remaining Miles.





Expected Remaining Mileage Based on Current Car Mileage.




Figure 9 above shows the relationship between expected remaining mileage and current mileage across the full range of simulated car lifetime mileages, whose distribution is shown in Figure 4. As expected, expected remaining mileage declines as current mileage increases and appears to follow a polynomial or exponential trend. This trend is clearest between 0 and 300,000 miles; however, beyond approximately 400,000 miles, the curve becomes increasingly jagged and more difficult to interpret.
This jaggedness is expected, as relatively few simulated vehicles survive to such high mileages. Recall from Figure 6 that at 400,000 miles, only 15 of the original 100,000 simulated vehicles remain. Because the calculation of mean residual life involves taking a mean, estimates based on a smaller number of observations are inherently more susceptible to random variation. Therefore, estimates of expected remaining mileage above 400,000 miles are inherently less stable than those at lower mileages, where more simulated vehicles remain. This increased variability contributes to the jaggedness observed toward the end of the curve in Figure 9. For these reasons, and because so few car survive beyond 400,000 miles, it would be appropriate to limit the model to 400,000 miles.
The resulting model is shown in Figure 10.





Expected Remaining Mileage Model with Current Mileage Filtered Up to 400,000 Miles.




As mentioned earlier, the relationship between expected remaining mileage and current mileage appears to follow either a polynomial or an exponential trend. Although identifying the underlying trend is not the main focus of this project, it would still be insightful to get a general idea of which model best captures the trend. Therefore, let us fit several models to the expected remaining mileage data and visually compare their fits to the expected remaining mileage curve to determine which model best captures the trend.





Identifying the Best-Fit Model for Expected Remaining Mileage Estimates




As observed in Figure 11, the cubic model appears to provide the best fit to the expected remaining mileage data and curve, out of all the models shown.

title: Inside the Language of SMS Spam: Characterizing Spam Messaging Using Regular Expression
text:
Introduction



Figure 1: SMS Message


Now we’ve all been there. After all, who can say no to a FREE $1,000? Just click the link!
In all reality, you probably shouldn’t click that link. This is yet another SMS spam message. SMS (Short Message Service) spam messages are unsolicited texts—messages not prompted by recipients—that are often sent in bulk to a large number of mobile phones. While often persuasive, deceptive, and sometimes indistinguishable from legitimate messages (like “Hi, I wanted to check up on you”), SMS spam messages can be more than an annoyance; they can also pose serious digital security risks.
Thus, it is natural to wonder: What exactly characterizes spam messages? What linguistic patterns might be more prominent in spam messages compared to legitimate ones? And how can we use this knowledge to better distinguish between spam and legitimate messages?
These are some of the questions this project seeks to tackle.


Data & Data Source
The SMS Spam Collection dataset contains 5,572 tagged SMS messages that have been collected for the purpose of SMS Spam research. Each message in the dataset is tagged as either ham—a legitimate message—or spam, to distinguish between the message types. Moreover, as we can observe from the bar chart below, less than 1,000 messages in the dataset are spam while all other messages are ham (legitimate messages).


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(stringi)
library(patchwork)
library(ggmosaic)
library(scales)

# Import dataset

sms <- read_csv("spam.csv")

sms <- sms |> 
    select("v1", "v2") |> 
    rename(Label = v1, Message = v2)

# Original dataset includes characters that R does not recongize, so let's change all such character to '`' which has no instances in the original dataset.

sms <- sms |> 
    mutate(Message = iconv(Message, from = "", to = "UTF-8", sub = "`"), Label = factor(Label, levels = c("spam", "ham")))

# From dataset, how many messages are ham vs spam?

sms_bar <- sms |> 
    ggplot(aes(x = Label)) +
    geom_bar(aes(fill = Label)) +
    labs(title = "Number of Observations By Message Type", x = "Message Type", y = "Count") +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16), axis.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14), axis.text = element_text(size = 13), legend.position = "none")

sms_bar









The dataset used in this project was downloaded from Kaggle; however, the original dataset was obtained from the UC Irvine Machine Learning Repository and can be found at the citation below:
Almeida, Tiago and Jos Hidalgo. “SMS Spam Collection.” UCI Machine Learning Repository, 2011, https://doi.org/10.24432/C5CC84.
The dataset is also available in the GitHub repository for this website.


Analysis: Characterizing SMS Spam Messages


Code
# Let's visualize message length (includes spaces) per message type

sms_box <- sms |> 
    ggplot(aes(x = Label, y = str_length(Message))) +
    geom_boxplot(aes(color = Label), alpha = 0.5) +
    labs(title = "Distribution of Message Length By Message Type", x = "Message Type", y = "Length of Message") +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16), axis.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14), axis.text = element_text(size = 13), legend.position = "none")

sms_box









Code
# Let's find the median message length for each message type

sms |> 
    group_by(Label) |> 
    summarize(Median = median(str_length(Message)))


# A tibble: 2 × 2
  Label Median
  <fct>  <int>
1 spam     149
2 ham       52


Code
# Median Length of Message for ham: 52 Characters
# Median length of Message for spam: 149 Characters


When analyzing the boxplots and table above, we observe that spam messages have a higher median length of 149 characters compared to ham messages, which have a median length of 52 characters. Additionally, we also observe that the distribution of spam message lengths is less variable and more concentrated than that of ham messages.


Code
# Let's visualize the proporation of "spam" words by message types. 

sms_words <- sms |> 
    mutate(Message = str_to_lower(Message)) |> 
    mutate(
        Free = str_detect(Message, "\\bfree\\b"),
        Win = str_detect(Message, "\\bwin\\b|\\bwon\\b"),
        Claim = str_detect(Message, "\\bclaim\\b"),
        Urgent = str_detect(Message, "\\burgent\\b"),
        Prize = str_detect(Message, "\\bprize\\b"),
        Call = str_detect(Message, "\\bcall\\b"),
        Now = str_detect(Message, "\\bnow\\b"),
        Reply = str_detect(Message, "\\breply\\b"),
        Congrats = str_detect(Message, "\\bcongrats\\b | \\bcongratulation(s)?\\b"),
        Activate = str_detect(Message, "\\bactivate\\b"),
        Private = str_detect(Message, "\\bprivate\\b"),
        Cash = str_detect(Message, "\\bcash\\b"),
        XXX = str_detect(Message, "\\bxxx\\b")
    ) 

sms_word <- pivot_longer(sms_words, Free:XXX, names_to = "Word", values_to = "Contains")

sms_word |> 
    filter(Contains) |> 
    count(Label, Word) |> 
    ggplot() +
    geom_mosaic(aes(x = Word, fill = Label, weight = n)) +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0,1, by = 0.10)) +
    labs(title = "Proportion of Spam-Associated Words by Message Type", subtitle = str_wrap("Each side column's widths on the y-axis represents the relative frequency of that word in the dataset, while the colored areas show the proporation of messages containing the word per message type.", width = 100), y = "Proporation of Messages", fill = "Message Type") +
    coord_flip() +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16), plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 14), axis.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14), axis.text = element_text(size = 13))









The mosaic plot above illustrates the proportion of spam and ham messages containing each spam-associated word, while also providing information about the relative frequency of each word in the dataset. As can be observed from the plot, more spam messages than ham messages contain the words: Win, Urgent, Reply, Prize, Private, Free, Claim, Cash, Call, and Activate. Additionally, the words Call, Free, Win, Relpy, and Claim, have higher relative frequencies than other the words, suggesting that these words are not only associated with spam messages but are also more commonly used across spam messages. Interestingly, the words Now, XXX, and Congrats/Congratulations appear more frequently in ham messages than spam messages, suggesting that these words may not be as useful in distinguishing between spam and ham messages.


Code
# Let's visualize repetition of specific symbols and words by message types. 

sms_duplicates <- sms |> 
    mutate(Message = str_to_lower(Message)) |>
    mutate(
        Exclam = str_count(Message, "!"),
        Money = str_count(Message, "\\$"),
        Free = str_count(Message, "\\bfree\\b"),
        Win = str_count(Message, "\\bwin\\b"),
        Cash = str_count(Message, "\\bcash\\b"),
        Call = str_count(Message, "\\bcall\\b"),
        Prize = str_count(Message, "\\bprize\\b")
    )

sms_dups <- sms_duplicates |> 
    pivot_longer(Exclam:Prize, names_to = "Expression", values_to = "Contains")


sms_dup_viz <- sms_dups |> 
    group_by(Label, Expression) |> 
    summarize(Mean_Repeats = mean(Contains)) |> 
    mutate(Expression = fct_relevel(factor(Expression), c("Exclam", "Call", "Free", "Prize", "Cash", "Win", "Money"))) |> 
    ggplot(aes(x = Mean_Repeats, y = Expression)) +
    geom_line() +
    geom_point(aes(color = Label), size = 4) +
    coord_flip() +
    labs(title = str_wrap("Difference in Mean Number of Repeats for Selected Words and Symbols Across Message Types", width = 80), x = "Mean Number of Repeats Per Message", color = "Message Type") +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0,1, by = 0.10)) +
    scale_y_discrete(labels = c("Exclam" = "!", "Money" = "$")) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16), axis.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14), axis.text = element_text(size = 13), legend.title = element_text(size = 13), legened.text = element_text(size = 13))

sms_dup_viz









From the graph above, we can start to understand the relationship between the repetition of specific words/symbol and message type. More specifically, we observe that spam messages have a far higher average number of repetitions for !, Call, Free than ham messages—although this was the general trend across all the selected symbols and words. This suggests that the number of repetitions of !, Call, Free may be particularly useful in determining if a message is spam or ham, as !, Call, Free have the greatest differences in average repetitions between the two message types.


Code
# Let's visualize monetary values used in messages by message type.


sms_moneys <- sms |> 
    mutate(Message = str_to_lower(Message)) |> 
    mutate(
        Pounds = parse_number(str_extract(Message, "\\d{0,3},?\\d{1,3}(?= pounds)")),
        Money = parse_number(str_extract(Message, "(?<=\\$)\\d{0,3},?\\d{1,3}")),
        Prize = parse_number(str_extract(Message, "\\d{0,3},?\\d{1,3}(?= prize)"))
    ) |> 
    pivot_longer(Pounds:Prize, names_to = "Expression", values_to = "Number")
    

sms_money_viz <- sms_moneys |>  
    ggplot(aes(x = Number, fill = Label)) +
    geom_histogram(na.rm = TRUE) +
    scale_x_log10(labels = label_comma()) +
    facet_grid(~Label) +
    labs(title = "Distribution of Monetary Values Used in Messages By Message Type", subtitle = str_wrap('Any values preceding the words "pounds" and "prize" (regardless of case), as well as any values following the "$" symbol, were considered monetary values.', width = 130), x = "Monetary Value", y = "Count", fill = "Message Type") +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16), axis.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14), axis.text = element_text(size = 13), legend.title = element_text(size = 13), legened.text = element_text(size = 13))


sms_money_viz









As seen in the histograms above, the most common monetary value used in spam messages is 1000, with most spam messages (that contain a monetary value) containing monetary values around this amount. On the other hand, the monetary values in ham messages are all less than 1000 and scattered, with no clear and common monetary value. This may be due to the smaller number of observations of ham messages that contain monetary values as compared to spam messages, which also suggests that spam messages are more likely to contain monetary values than ham messages. Lastly, it is important to note that for values preceding “pounds,” the use of pounds as a unit of mass could also have been included as a monetary value, meaning that the “4” in a message stating “I want 4 pounds of apples” could have been extracted as a monetary value.


Conclusion
Although several characteristics of spam messages were explored, let’s now bring them all together and summarize our findings.
Based on the dataset we utilized and the analysis completed, we can generally characterize spam messages linguistically and physically as:

Having a length of ~132.5-157 characters (Q1 and Q3 of boxplot).
Containing words such as Win, Urgent, Reply, Prize, Private, Free, Claim, Cash, Call, and Activate.
Containing higher than average number of repetitions of !, Call, Free.
Containing monetary values of 1,000 or around 1,000.

Therefore, by identifying the patterns and characteristics that distinguish spam messages from ham messages, our analysis has helped establish a clearer definition of spam messages and a general criteria for distinguishing between the two message types.

title: Affect of Psilocybin Mushroom Consumption on Difficult Mental Arithmetic Score
text:
2 Methods
Planned study design: We will be using an experimental study design. Half of our experiment’s participants will be randomly assigned to receive 10 grams of Psilocybin Mushrooms, while the other half will be assigned to the control group that will not receive any Psilocybin Mushrooms.
The target population/participants: We will attempt to generalize our results to all adults (defined as over 18 years old for purposes of this study) on the islands.
The inclusion and exclusion criteria: Our only exclusion criterion is individuals under the age of 18, due to the ethical dilemmas that providing psychedelics to individuals under 18–like children–might pose.
The sampling methods: We will be using random sampling and random assignment. We are going to use two random number generators to select a city and a household, and then randomly pick an adult from that household to be a participant. From all the individuals selected, half will be assigned to the treatment group and the other half will be assigned to the control group. We will try to roughly sample the same number of individuals from each island.
The intervention(s): The consumption/lack of consumption of Psilocybin mushrooms (2 levels).
The outcome(s) to be measured: The score received on a difficult mental arithmetic exam (quantitative).
Other demographic variables collected: We will record information on age, gender, wealth, and island of residence for each participant in our study.
The sample size calculation and justification: See “Summary of Power Analysis and Sample Size Determination” section
The randomization (random assignment) methods: We are using random sampling and random assignment, as described above under sampling methods
The blinding methods: We will not be using blinding methods, since us (the researchers) knowing the assignment of the explanatory variable has no effect on the response variable, and we didn’t have an option to use a placebo for a single-blind test (and using something else as a placebo could have an effect we are unfamiliar with due to the digital format of this study).
The study implementation: We will randomly sample individuals from the islands as outlined above, half of the individuals will take mushrooms (1 minute), and then after the conclusion of the consumption, those individuals will take the ‘Mental Arithmetic Difficult’ test (4 mins). The other half of randomly sampled individuals will only take the ‘Mental Arithmetic Difficult’ test (4 mins).
The statistical methods used to analyze the data: Two-sample T-test.
